Sam Liccardo (D) is the strongest candidate for this United States House seat. On July 14, 2026, he cosponsored the Block the Bombs Act, and he opposes the $3.3 billion in offensive weapons funding to Israel, pledging to vote against the appropriations bill carrying it. In July 2025 he called for immediate humanitarian aid to Gaza and criticized U.S. military support for Israel's actions, and in August 2025 he told South San Jose residents their anger over Palestinian suffering was justified. CAIR Action has named him their preferred candidate, and WhoFundsMyRep reports no AIPAC PAC or UDP money behind him. He has not called the war a genocide, voted against the Massie Amendment that would have eliminated the $3.3 billion in Israel aid, and backs $500 million for Iron Dome and Arrow 3. Even with those shortfalls, his concrete acts—cosponsoring the Block the Bombs Act, opposing offensive weapons funding, and publicly validating Palestinian community anger—make him the clearest choice for voters who want Congress to end arms transfers to Israel and deliver humanitarian aid to Gaza.

In this race for the United States Senate, Ty Pinkins (I) is the stronger candidate. He has not called the war in Gaza a genocide and has not backed any measure to block weapons transfers or end military aid to Israel. What he has done is call Trump's 2025 Gaza plan reckless in a February 2025 campaign release and, in October 2026, declare that the relationship between the United States and Israel's government is unhealthy, while publicly committing to reject AIPAC money. For a federal office, his silence on ending arms sales effectively preserves the status quo. But his opponent, Cindy Hyde-Smith (R), has spent years defending Israel, cosponsored the 2025 Antisemitism Awareness Act, posted that most Gazans viewed the October 7 attack as correct, blocked Gazan refugee admission, and took over a quarter of a million dollars from AIPAC and United Democracy Project. Pinkins is the only candidate here who has spoken against the current course and refused the money that shapes it.

Alani Bankhead has not called the war in Gaza a genocide and has not backed a full end to U.S. military and economic aid to Israel; her July 2026 podcast remarks expressed strong personal affinity for the IDF and Mossad, and even her October 2026 call to enforce the Leahy Law as a complete arms embargo during the assault remains a conditional, narrow restriction rather than a structural break from U.S. support. In a federal race, that combination effectively leaves the status quo of open-ended U.S. backing to Israel largely undisturbed. Still, Bankhead is the strongest candidate on this Montana U.S. Senate ballot because no other listed contender carries a single documented position on Palestinian lives or U.S. weapons transfers. Her October 2026 Leahy Law stance is the only concrete act in this race that would restrict arms reaching a theater of ongoing civilian harm, and her willingness to name a specific legal mechanism, even while stopping short of a full condemnation, marks a measurable difference from candidates who have said nothing at all on these questions.

For the United States Senate seat in West Virginia, Rachel Fetty Anderson is the strongest choice. She has not called the war in Gaza a genocide and has not moved to end aid to Israel specifically, so her position is a partial step rather than a full break. But she has stated she would not vote to send or sell weapons to any country except for purely self-defense purposes, a stance that directly constrains the arms pipeline to Israel in a way neither of her opponents does. Shelley Moore Capito cosponsored the 2025 Antisemitism Awareness Act, wiring the IHRA definition into federal campus investigations and embedding the framework that equates criticism of Israel with antisemitism into the Education Department. S. Marshall Wilson told voters in a November 2024 questionnaire that Israel's worldview aligns more closely with the American Founding than any other Middle East nation, offering no engagement with Palestinian justice or the war in Gaza. Anderson's two-state solution and self-defense-only weapons stance make her the only candidate in this race whose stated positions pull policy away from the status quo the other two reinforce.

Dr. Richard Pan has not called the war in Gaza a genocide and has not backed blocking weapons transfers or ending U.S. aid to Israel; his platform calls generically for ending wars without naming Israel, and for a U.S. Representative that effectively supports the status quo of American backing for the Israeli government. In the August 17 Sacramento Bee debate he repeatedly declined a yes-or-no answer on genocide, affirming instead Israel's right to defend itself while acknowledging the humanitarian crisis. He remains the strongest option in this race. His opponent Kevin Kiley traveled to Israel on an AIPAC-organized delegation in April 2024, praised Yale's overnight crackdown on pro-Palestine student encampments in April 2025, and voted to incorporate the IHRA definition into federal education law, while taking $74,799 from pro-Israel PACs in the 2026 cycle alone. CAIR Action lists Pan as preferred, and the UDP-funded 314 Action Fund spent roughly $1.2 million in independent support for his campaign. Pan named the humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza; Kiley spent those same months defending a university's crackdown on the students who protested it.

Shannon Taylor has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, has not backed a vote to block U.S. weapons transfers, and at a September 2026 rally gave no answer when asked about Palestine. For a candidate seeking the U.S. House of Representatives, that silence on American military and economic support effectively sustains the status quo. Still, Taylor is the stronger choice. On the first anniversary of October 7, 2024, she called for an immediate ceasefire, hostage release, and a rebuilding plan, naming innocent lives in Israel and Gaza. She has not endorsed an arms embargo but insists U.S. military aid must follow international law and civilian protection. Contrast Robert Wittman, who voted Yea on the 2024 Antisemitism Awareness Act embedding the IHRA definition in Title VI education enforcement, sponsored its 2025 successor, and signed an October 2025 letter calling ICJ genocide proceedings a redefinition effort targeting Israel and empowering Hamas. Taylor draws AFGE and AFSCME labor backing but has not taken the concrete legislative steps voters need, and that gap should weigh in their decision.

For the United States House seat in Nebraska's second district, Denise Powell is the candidate who turned her back on the pro-Israel establishment when it came calling. In April 2026 she rejected an ad buy from Democratic Majority for Israel, and in May she disavowed support from all Israel-focused outside groups, prompting DMFI to cancel its spending in the race. Jewish Insider identified her as the Israel critic in the Nebraska Democratic primary. That said, she has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers to Israel, and has not taken a recorded vote on U.S. military or economic aid, and for a federal office-seeker, taking no position on those questions effectively supports the status quo. Yet the AIPAC-linked groups BOLD America and EDW Action Fund poured over six hundred thousand dollars into her campaign despite her disavowal, showing that the pro-Israel machinery views her as its fundable option even as she pushes back. That makes Powell the strongest choice in this race.

In the California State Assembly district 18 race, Mia Bonta is the strongest option for voters who want a representative who pushes back against legislation that chills speech about Palestine. On AB 715, the antisemitism-coordinator and classroom-material oversight bill whose floor debate centered on speech about Palestine, Bonta publicly registered skepticism and pressed co-authors to clean up the text after its late-night passage, then ultimately voted aye. She has not called the war in Gaza a genocide and has not backed any measure to block weapons transfers or cut military aid to Israel. Still, she is the only candidate here with documented engagement on the question: CAIR Action preferred her, AROC Action endorsed her, and her willingness to publicly challenge the rushed handling of AB 715 shows a legislator willing to push back rather than simply follow the chamber. Her platform carries no Palestine-specific policy statement, but the community-aligned endorsements and her floor conduct set her apart from every other candidate in this race.

Patrick Ahrens is the strongest option for California State Assembly, District 26, in the November 2026 general. On the two questions that matter most—opposing the genocide in Gaza and ending U.S. military and economic aid to Israel—Ahrens has not called the violence a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers, and has not voted against aid bills. What he has done is earn the trust of the communities most directly affected: CAIR Action lists him as its preferred candidate and Vote for Peace rates him an Ally, assessments that carry weight even where his floor work on classroom content, including his Aye on the antisemitism-coordinator bill AB 715 and his co-authorship of the failed AB 1468, sits in tension with those community positions. A candidate who has been vetted and put forward by the Palestinian and Muslim organizations most directly impacted by U.S. policy toward Israel gives a voter a concrete, grounded reason to trust the district will be represented in a way that reflects those communities' priorities, and in this race that makes Ahrens the clear choice.

For Illinois governor in November 2026, JB Pritzker has taken concrete steps to push back on U.S. arms flows to Israel. In August 2025 he endorsed Senate resolutions to block U.S. arms sales to Israel, calling it the right kind of message to pressure Netanyahu on Gaza's humanitarian crisis, and in March 2026 he broke from AIPAC, labeling its seventy-million-dollar Illinois spending as interference and saying he wants no part of it. Pritzker has not called the violence in Gaza a genocide, and in May 2026 he said criticism of Israel is crossing into antisemitism, while in 2024 he downplayed Chicago's Gaza ceasefire resolution for not holding Hamas accountable. Even so, among the candidates listed, Pritzker is the only one who has backed blocking weapons transfers and publicly rejected AIPAC's influence. Darren Bailey, by contrast, declared in October 2023 that he has always stood with Israel, calling Hamas a despicable terrorist organization, without any mention of civilian harm or conditions on U.S. support. For a voter who wants to see pressure on arms sales and a break from Israel-aligned lobbying, Pritzker is the stronger choice.

Shelby has not called the Gaza war a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers to Israel, and has not taken divestment action; his one public statement, in August 2026, dismissed Governor Huckabee's Israel pledges as a distraction from Arkansas food insecurity and infant mortality, a bluntly negative framing toward US-Israel diplomacy that stops short of engaging Palestinian justice or the Gaza crisis. Still, in this race for Arkansas governor, the alternatives carry concrete, escalating commitments to Israel. Fredrick Love, in May 2023, sponsored Arkansas Senate Resolution 60 commending Israel on its 75th anniversary and affirming the Israeli people's right to defend their country. Sarah Huckabee Sanders signed SB 352 embedding the IHRA definition into school and university conduct codes, committed twenty-five to fifty million dollars of state money to Israeli government bonds, met Netanyahu and called the Arkansas-Israel bond unbreakable, then in October 2026 declared Arkansas makes no apology for standing with Israel while branding it disgusting and shameful to raise October 7 alongside any criticism of Israel. Shelby has done none of that, and his stated priority on domestic economic distress over Israel diplomacy makes him the clearest break from the pro-Israel path the other candidates have built.

Dan Ahlers is the strongest choice for Governor of South Dakota because he is the only candidate whose public record centers Palestinian civilian lives and calls for pressure on Israel to stop killing them. As SDDP Executive Director in May 2024, he directed a party statement acknowledging the October 7 attack while emphasizing more than thirty thousand Gaza civilian deaths and urging continued pressure on Israel to end hostilities. To be clear, Ahlers has not called the situation a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers, and has not called for ending U.S. military support to Israel. Even so, among the candidates here, he alone has put Palestinian civilian harm at the center of a public position and urged action against Israel. Rhoden, by contrast, led South Dakota's first trade delegation to Israel in June 2025, met President Herzog, Knesset Speaker Ohana, and Foreign Minister Sa'ar, called Israel a key partner in the state's economic success, and brought defense businesses actively seeking Israeli market sales. That deepens economic entanglement with the country carrying out the bombardment rather than applying any pressure.

Jocelyn Benson has not called the war in Gaza a genocide or voted to block weapons transfers to Israel. Still, for Michigan governor she remains the strongest option listed. In January 2025 she issued a public statement on the Israel-Hamas ceasefire, and in October 2023 Arab-American leaders called her synagogue dance during the initial Gaza strikes tone-deaf, evidence that community accountability reaches her in ways it does not reach her opponents. Anthony Hudson voted against the February 2024 border bill partly over its Israel funding yet still supports U.S. aid for Israel's defense. John James has called himself a staunch supporter of Israel, introduced a bill to expand U.S. security cooperation with Israel, received over two hundred thousand dollars from AIPAC-aligned PACs, and frames the conflict as eliminating Hamas and Iranian proxies. Benson is the only candidate here whose record shows responsiveness to Palestinian community pressure without locking in a security-first, pro-arms posture.

For California's Superintendent of Public Instruction, Richard Barrera is the strongest option in this November 2026 race. Barrera has not called Israel's conduct in Gaza a genocide, has not called for a ceasefire, and has not backed blocking weapons transfers. Even so, he is the candidate most willing to push back on the state's antisemitism enforcement framework: at a 2026 superintendent forum he expressed concerns about AB 715's classroom effects and declined to commit to defending the bill against every lawsuit, saying he would defend it only when that protects students. CAIR Action listed him Preferred, a tier short of full endorsement, and Vote for Peace rated him Neutral. By contrast, Sonja Shaw pressed for stronger AB 715 enforcement at that same forum, criticized a fellow candidate's abstention, and in March 2024, as Chino Valley Unified School Board president, refused to let a pro-Palestinian group address the board while other districts passed ceasefire resolutions. Vote for Peace opposed Shaw in the general. Barrera's willingness to question AB 715's scope and his Preferred standing with CAIR Action make him the clearer choice for a superintendent who will not treat that enforcement bill as beyond scrutiny.

For the City Council Member — At-large race in Walnut Creek on November 3, 2026, Cherise Marie Khaund is the only candidate with a documented record of engaging with the humanitarian crisis in Gaza. On October 11, 2023, she shared educator resources for discussing the Israel-Gaza conflict, drew on her time with peace activists from both sides, and highlighted that over one million children in Gaza lack clean water, food, and healthcare. She has not called the crisis a genocide, has not named Israel as the responsible party, and has not called for an end to U.S. military aid to Israel. Still, in a field where no other candidate has any researched record on the issue, Khaund is the only person in this race who has taken a public, documented stand centering Palestinian children's suffering and who has worked alongside peace activists from both sides to bring that reality into public discourse. For voters who want a representative who at minimum will not look away from the crisis, she is the clearest choice on the ballot.

For City Council Member, District 2, Desrie Campbell authored Fremont's March 2024 statement urging meaningful dialogue to halt the hostilities and a lasting and just solution for both Israel and Gaza. Campbell has not called the war a genocide, has not supported any measure to block weapons transfers or end U.S. military and economic aid to Israel, and when the council considered adding permanent ceasefire language to that statement, Campbell refused, calling it divisive. The equidistant framing means the statement condemns humanitarian harm without assigning responsibility to Israel, and that refusal to commit to ending military action is a real shortfall that voters should weigh. Even so, Campbell is the strongest option in this race: the statement at least forces Fremont to name the killing and demand a just resolution rather than fall silent, and a councilmember who will sit in a chamber and push for dialogue on behalf of Gaza, however measured the language, gives voters a point of leverage that silence does not. Support Campbell.

For the at-large Los Gatos Town Council seat in November, Rob Stump has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers to Israel, and has not taken divestment action. That silence is a real gap. But the Bay Area Muslim Council's opposition to Stump is pointed squarely at his tenure as a planning commissioner, where they called him the worst they had seen in that role, and it is not a judgment on his stance toward Palestinians. Mary Badame, by contrast, drew opposition from the same group with a direct advisory tied to her record on Palestinian justice and Israel policy, meaning she took a position on those issues that community advocates found contrary. When the choice is between a candidate with no contrary action on the Palestine question and one whose record on that question drew explicit Muslim-community opposition, Stump is the stronger option for a voter holding candidates to the tests of opposing the genocide in Gaza and ending U.S. military and economic aid to Israel. He is not a champion on that front, but he is not the candidate who moved against that community when the moment came.

Ruth Ferguson is the strongest candidate for the San Francisco Community College District Trustee seat on the November 2026 ballot. On the conflict in Gaza, her sole public statement, a co-authored op-ed from October 20, 2023, condemned harmful rhetoric following the Israel attack and the Gaza siege, framing the crisis through Jewish-Muslim safety and mutual justice. She has not called the violence a genocide, called for a ceasefire, addressed Palestinian civilian casualties by name, or backed blocking weapons transfers or ending U.S. aid to Israel. What makes her the strongest choice here is that she is the only candidate in this race with a documented public record, and that record shows a voice for the safety of Jewish and Muslim San Franciscans rather than silence, paired with a campaign platform focused entirely on City College education policy. Voters who want a trustee who has actually spoken publicly on community safety and who centers local education can weigh a concrete, dated text against an empty slate.

For the November 2026 general election for California's 17th congressional district, Ro Khanna is the candidate who has acted. He issued a ceasefire statement in 2024, and BAMC Action called his genocide recognition in Gaza a game changer. On June 4, 2026, he introduced an amendment to strike U.S.-Israel military integration from the NDAA. On July 1, 2026, he co-sponsored the Block the Bombs Act and a measure to eliminate $3.3 billion in military aid to Israel, declaring Zero Aid to Israel. His January 2026 Yea on a foreign-aid package, which he attributed to snuck provisions, is outweighed by these concrete acts. Khanna is endorsed by CAIR Action, AROC Action, and Citizens Against AIPAC Corruption. By contrast, Ritesh Tandon rejects the genocide label, called Khanna's ceasefire support naive and a policy of timidity, and tags pro-Israel organizations. Khanna is the only candidate in this race who has moved to end the weapons and the war.

For the United States House of Representatives seat in California's 8th congressional district, John Garamendi has moved decisively on the questions voters care about most. On July 28, 2025, he called Israel's actions in Gaza a genocide being committed against the people of Palestine and confirmed he voted against military support for Israel. He sponsors the Block the Bombs Act, and in July 2025 he demanded an end to the starvation crisis in Gaza and held Israel accountable for settler violence against Palestinian activists. He takes no funding from AIPAC or its allied lobbying groups, and CAIR Action lists him as a Preferred candidate. No other candidate in this race has demonstrated comparable action on opposing the genocide or blocking U.S. weapons transfers.

For U.S. Representative in California's 10th District, Mark DeSaulnier (D) has taken concrete steps to end U.S. military support for Israel's war in Gaza. He voted No on successive Israel aid bills through 2025 and 2026, voted Yes on the Massie amendment eliminating $3.3 billion in military aid, and sponsors the Block the Bombs Act. In July 2025 he stated he no longer votes for offensive military aid to Israel and called the situation in Gaza unacceptable by any standards of humanity, urging an immediate halt to military operations and delivery of food and humanitarian aid. CAIR Action endorsed him, and WhoFundsMyRep reports he has received no AIPAC or DMFI PAC money. He has not sponsored genocide-recognition language, and earlier Yes votes on UNRWA funding cuts, a PLO entry ban, and the Boulder resolution complicate his record, yet no other candidate in this race has a documented track record of voting against arms transfers and calling for an end to hostilities. J Street PAC also endorsed him.

Connie Chan is the strongest candidate for the U.S. House of Representatives in CD-11 because she has taken concrete, consistent action on the two questions that matter most. In January 2026 she pledged to co-sponsor the Block the Bombs Act, demanding a full arms embargo and the end of all U.S. military aid to Israel, and she told The Intercept she would not fund Iron Dome. As a San Francisco Supervisor she voted in the 8-3 supermajority for a sustained Gaza ceasefire in January 2024, and she has consistently called the war a genocide. Her campaign carries a standing pledge to reject money from AIPAC and its lobbyists. By contrast, Scott Wiener supported Iron Dome sales, opposed local ceasefire resolutions as early as February 2024, and co-authored California's antisemitism-education bill that CAIR warned could silence Palestine teaching. Wiener only acknowledged the genocide label in a January 2026 video after refusing to answer the question at a debate. Chan has the backing of CAIR Action and AROC Action, and she is the candidate whose record aligns with ending the war and cutting off the weapons pipeline.

Vote for Lateefah Simon for U.S. Representative in the 12th district. Simon has taken concrete legislative action on both questions that matter most: she sponsors the Block the Bombs Act to halt U.S. arms transfers to Israel and voted for the Massie amendment eliminating $3.3 billion in military aid to Israel, while her official House page in September 2025 called for an end to genocide in Gaza. She rejects AIPAC, DMFI, and Lockheed Martin campaign funding, and Track AIPAC, CAIR Action, and AROC Action all endorse her. She did vote for the Boulder resolution, which conflated anti-Zionism with antisemitic violence, a step that weakens her record on protecting Palestinian expression. Jamie Joyce also calls Gaza a genocide and refuses Pro-Israel PAC money, but her FARA proposal targets AIPAC's lobbying activity rather than the U.S. military relationship with Israel, and her campaign pledge to end war does not specify an Israel or Gaza policy. Simon's record contains the actual votes and bills that directly reduce American weapons flowing into Gaza, making her the stronger choice on the two questions voters are weighing.

For Aisha Wahab to represent the people of California's 14th district in the United States House of Representatives, voters should weigh what each candidate has actually done. Wahab called the killing of Palestinians in Gaza a genocide at an April 2026 forum, cosponsored the Block the Bombs Act to halt weapons transfers, and on August 18, 2026, introduced a California Senate resolution demanding an end to the war she described as a genocide. She won the 2026 special election against millions in pro-Israel attack advertising, framing the result as proof the district cannot be bought. Her community backing includes CAIR Action and AROC Action. Her opponent, Melissa Hernandez, declined to label Israel's actions in Gaza as genocide at that same April forum and received millions in independent spending from United Democracy Project and BOLD America, an AIPAC-linked super PAC network. Hernandez also carries an endorsement from a Hindutva-aligned Hindu American PAC. Wahab has not voted to end ongoing U.S. military aid to Israel beyond the Block the Bombs Act she cosponsored, but she has named the violence what it is and acted to stop the weapons that sustain it.

For the U.S. House of Representatives seat in California's 17th district, Ro Khanna has taken the most concrete action of any candidate on the two questions voters should weigh first. In June 2026 he introduced an amendment to strike the NDAA provision deepening U.S.-Israeli military integration, arguing it rewards Netanyahu. On July 1, 2026 he co-sponsored the Block the Bombs Act to stop U.S. military funding to Israel, declared a Zero Aid to Israel position, and criticized the Rules Committee for blocking a floor vote. He has called for a Gaza ceasefire since at least May 2024 and recognized the war as genocide. Muslim-community and pro-Palestine-aligned groups including CAIR Action, AROC Action, and Citizens Against AIPAC Corruption endorse him. His opponent Ritesh Tandon rejects the genocide label, calls Khanna's ceasefire support a policy of timidity, and accuses him of Muslim Brotherhood influence. Khanna is the stronger choice for a representative who will work to end U.S. arms and aid to Israel.

For the U.S. House of Representatives, Sam Liccardo is the strongest candidate in CD-16. He cosponsored the Block the Bombs Act (H.R. 3565) in July 2026, condemned U.S. military support for Israel's actions and called for immediate humanitarian aid to Gaza in July 2025, and validated the anger of South San Jose residents over the plight of Palestinians at an August 2025 town hall. CAIR Action lists him as a preferred candidate, and no AIPAC PAC or UDP money supports his campaign. Liccardo has not called the violence in Gaza a genocide, voted against the Massie amendment that would have eliminated $3.3 billion in Israel aid, and voted for a resolution conflating anti-Zionism with antisemitism. As the only candidate with a stated record in this race, his opposition to $3.3 billion in offensive weapons funding, his Block the Bombs cosponsorship, and his commitment to voting against the larger appropriations bill this cycle represent the furthest recorded movement toward pulling back U.S. military and economic entanglement with Israel's war.

For the race for United States Representative in CD-18 on November 3, 2026, Zoe Lofgren is the strongest candidate on the record. In 2026 she voted against $3.3 billion in Israeli military aid and sponsored the Block the Bombs Act, a marked shift from 2024, when she backed a $14 billion weapons package and voted to cut UNRWA funding. In July 2025 she called Gaza a humanitarian catastrophe, blamed Netanyahu for famine, and demanded U.S. pressure toward a two-state solution. She has not called the war a genocide or sponsored a recognition bill, and in a federal seat that silence effectively endorses the status quo. Even so, her 2026 vote against arms funding and her Block the Bombs sponsorship are the strongest concrete actions in this race. CAIR Action lists her as its preferred candidate and J Street PAC has endorsed her; WhoFundsMyRep shows no AIPAC or UDP money in her campaign. She signed the October 2023 de-escalation letter and the November 2023 settler-violence letter, and in January 2024 urged a permanent ceasefire and a massive increase in humanitarian aid to Palestinian civilians.

Everett Wess for United States Senator from Alabama is the stronger choice in this race, though his 2026 platform has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, has not backed blocking U.S. weapons transfers, and his silence on American military and economic aid to Israel amounts to supporting the status quo for a federal office-holder. What he has done is put Palestinian rights, a ceasefire, and a two-state solution on the table. That is a step the other candidate will not take. Barry Moore has received $34,174 from pro-Israel PACs including $30,174 from AIPAC and United Democracy Project, voted to embed the IHRA definition in federal law, introduced a bill extending that language into civil-rights enforcement, and called for changing what Palestinian children are taught. Moore's record is one of alignment with Israeli government interests at every turn. Wess at least acknowledges Palestinian suffering and a path to two states, and his broader platform centers domestic priorities. For a Senate seat that shapes arms and aid policy, Wess is the candidate most likely to shift the conversation, even if his platform stops short of a full break.

For Colorado voters choosing their U.S. Senator in November 2026, Adam Withrow (UP) is the strongest option because his platform calls for an immediate stop to U.S. weapons transfers to Israel, arguing that self-defense does not justify killing or annexing sovereign neighbors. He frames his foreign policy as anti-war on all fronts, opposing the propping up of brutal regimes and the funding of conflicts, and supports a two-state solution on pre-1967 borders. He has not called the violence in Gaza a genocide by name. But his stated position to halt arms transfers is the most direct challenge to the status quo on the list. John Hickenlooper (D), by contrast, voted with the Republican majority to defeat two resolutions that would have partially blocked military aid to Israel, cosponsored the 2025 Antisemitism Awareness Act directing the IHRA definition for campus investigations, and in June 2025 framed a memorial around antisemitism rather than Gaza. Hickenlooper has also drawn $325,235 from AIPAC PAC and United Democracy Project in the 2026 cycle. Withrow's platform puts stopping weapons transfers first; Hickenlooper's record shows votes against blocking them.

In the 2026 Georgia Senate race, Jon Ossoff is the strongest candidate for voters who want to end U.S. military aid to Israel. On April 15, 2026, he voted to advance resolutions blocking sales of 1,000-lb bomb bodies and military bulldozers to Israel, and in November 2024 he voted in favor of resolutions blocking further weapons transfers, framing the action as protest against disproportionate retaliation killing tens of thousands. In May 2021, he led 29 senators in a joint letter urging an immediate ceasefire. He has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, deferring that determination to the International Criminal Court, though he affirmed on the Senate floor and to constituents that the IDF violated laws of war. Ossoff received no money from AIPAC PAC or United Democracy Project. His opponent, Mike Collins, states his faith compels him to support Israel, rebukes Ossoff for voting against weapons sales, and drew $19,146 from AIPAC PAC and United Democracy Project. Vote for Peace, which evaluates candidates on human-rights and war-lobby grounds, backs Ossoff and opposes Collins.

Angie Nixon is the strongest candidate for United States Senator from Florida. In November 2023 she introduced House Resolution 31C calling for an immediate cease-fire in Israel and occupied Palestine and was the sole lawmaker to cite Palestinian deaths in debate. On the floor she told colleagues who turned their backs that she was on the right side of history because she did not want the babies to die. After winning her primary in August 2026, she called Netanyahu a war criminal and opposed sending Israel U.S. money or weapons at this moment. Her platform commits to ending U.S. support for West Bank settlements. She has not called the war a genocide, but her concrete cease-fire legislation and stated opposition to U.S. arms and funding make her the clearest choice. Ashley Moody voted against blocking arms transfers to Israel in July 2025, co-sponsored the Stand with Israel Act in May 2025, and drew over half a million dollars from AIPAC-affiliated PACs. Nixon carries pro-Palestine-aligned backing from Representative Ro Khanna.

Josh Turek has not called the killing of Palestinians in Gaza a genocide, has not voted to block U.S. weapons shipments, and has not demanded an end to military aid to Israel. For a federal seat in the U.S. Senate, that silence effectively upholds the status quo on the two questions voters most need answered. What Turek has done is back, by September 2025, conditions on U.S. support for Israel that demand accountability on American policy, and his campaign centers economic, healthcare, and civil-liberties priorities. Ro Khanna has endorsed him. Ashley Hinson, by contrast, voted Yea on all three Israel Security Supplemental Appropriations Acts and on H.R. 6090, declared in August 2025 that Hamas is one hundred percent to blame for the suffering in Gaza and that she will always stand with Israel, issued a press release in 2024 declaring Biden has abandoned Israel, and in October 2026 defended her vote against a measure to end the Iran war. A senator who conditions aid is a step away from one who funds every war without question.

Matt Loesby has not called the Gaza war a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers, and has not taken divestment action, and in a federal Senate race that silence on the two most direct levers effectively leaves the current trajectory in place. What Loesby has done is sharper in its diagnosis: in 2024 he named the Gaza war an elite power struggle, identifying a Neocon-Zionist faction allied with pro-Israel elements of the progressive coalition as a united force crushing those who stand with Gazan Palestinians, and in July 2026 he publicly questioned why a New Jersey representative was meddling in Malaysia's immigration policy toward Israeli citizens, signaling outright skepticism of US political engagement on Israel-related foreign policy. Jim Risch, by contrast, introduced the Senate companion to the NOPE Act blocking UN funding for Palestine beyond observer status, introduced a bill to defend Israel at the United Nations, told the floor that Gaza's suffering belongs to Hamas, called the humanitarian crisis not Israel's fault, and formally opposed allied nations recognizing a Palestinian state. Between a candidate who names the structural forces behind Palestinian harm and one who legislates to shield Israel from accountability, the choice is clear.

Adam Hamilton is the strongest candidate for Kansas's United States Senate seat. He has stated he would end offensive military aid to Israel and, in an October 2026 POLITICO interview, described voting to stop weapons transfers, saying he does not want tax-funded bombs dropped on innocent people. That said, Hamilton has not called Gaza a genocide, and his plan preserves defensive weapons transfers rather than ending all arms aid. Even so, no other candidate in this race comes close. Incumbent Roger Marshall demanded a fourteen-billion-dollar standalone Israel aid package on the Senate floor in November 2023, said in May 2024 that the U.S. should not accept Palestinian refugees from Gaza, and in April 2026 voted against a war-powers resolution to withdraw U.S. forces from the Iran conflict. Marshall's record is one of unqualified support for Israeli military operations and expanded American involvement. Hamilton, while falling short on the genocide label and full divestment, is the only candidate in this race moving toward restricting U.S. military entanglement and protecting Palestinian lives.

In the race for Kentucky's U.S. Senate seat on November 3, 2026, Charles Booker (D) is the strongest option listed. At a March 17, 2026 televised primary debate, Booker called Israel's actions in Gaza a genocide and said the United States should not fund them. That direct naming of what is happening and his clear rejection of U.S. military and economic support place him squarely on the two questions voters must ask: does this candidate oppose the genocide, and does he oppose funding it? His broader campaign platform commits to ending reckless wars, which extends and reinforces the specific stance he took at the debate. Vote for Peace, a pro-Palestine-aligned group, rated him an Ally heading into the general election. Booker's words at the debate are concrete and dated, and his platform commitment pushes the logic beyond a single statement, giving voters a coherent, actionable reason to back him.

Vote for Troy Jackson in the United States Senate race in Maine. On September 29, 2026, at a town hall he called Israel's actions in Gaza a genocide, named Netanyahu a war criminal to be prosecuted, and refused to vote for additional bombs or aid. Before the July 2026 nominating convention he pledged never to vote for U.S. taxpayer-funded military aid to Israel, and at the October 2026 general-election debate he opposed giving Israel a blank check, saying he did not want offensive weapons going to murder people in Palestine. Susan Collins, by contrast, defended current U.S. military aid to Israel as good in a 2026 debate, remains a very strong supporter of Israel, and drew $3,485,087 from the AIPAC PAC and its UDP arm, ranking first among one hundred senators for pro-Israel PAC money. Jackson sidestepped the issue at his July nomination speech and apologized after backlash over remarks about Jewish Maine residents, but his concrete acts—naming the genocide, refusing arms, vowing never to approve aid—set him apart from a candidate who calls that aid good and accepts its top dollar.

For the United States Senate, Ed Markey is the strongest choice on Gaza. In April 2026 he voted to advance S.J. Res. 32 and S.J. Res. 138, blocking sales of military bulldozers and 1,000-pound bomb bodies to Israel, and in his September 2026 primary victory speech he called to stop the bombing in Gaza and slash the Pentagon budget. He has not called what is happening in Gaza a genocide, and his arms votes target specific weapons rather than ending all U.S. aid to Israel. But those votes are concrete obstruction, and his 2021 co-signing of the Senate ceasefire resolution with 27 colleagues shows a sustained posture. Massachusetts Peace Action calls him a consistent opponent of arms enabling the slaughter in Gaza. Ro Khanna endorsed him, and as of October 2026 he had taken zero dollars from AIPAC PAC or United Democracy Project. Against Deaton, who declared Israel has the absolute right to defend itself and that supporting Israel serves American interests, Markey has actually voted to block weapons from reaching Gaza and is the only candidate in this field with recorded legislative action on these questions.

In the 2026 U.S. Senate race in Minnesota, Peggy Flanagan stands apart as the candidate who has confronted the violence in Gaza directly. In August 2026, she publicly accused Israel of genocide, stated she would have voted to cut off U.S. military aid, and said she would oppose offensive weapons sales to Israel. She also made her opponent's AIPAC support a campaign issue, putting war-lobby money in the spotlight. That record is backed by a Muslim-community and pro-Palestine-aligned endorsement from Rep. Ro Khanna. Her opponent, Michele Tafoya, did the opposite: during an October 16, 2026 debate she declared that there is no genocide happening in Gaza, and FEC filings show her campaign accepted money from a pro-Israel PAC. For a federal office where silence on these questions effectively endorses the status quo, Flanagan is the only candidate here who has named the crisis, committed to cutting off military funding, and refused to treat Israel-related funding as a nonissue.

Abdul El-Sayed is the strongest candidate for the U.S. Senate seat from Michigan. In October 2026 he accused Israel of genocide, and in February 2024 he called for an immediate ceasefire in Gaza. At a debate that October he called the Israel-versus-Iran threat question ridiculous and said Israel is dragging the United States into conflicts it should not be fighting, while an August 2026 Forward op-ed set out his two-state self-determination plan. His record does not yet show a specific vote against an Israeli arms appropriation or a cosponsored divestment bill, but his consistent opposition to U.S. war involvement and explicit genocide language put him on the right side of both tests in practice. Muslim-community backing from Ro Khanna, Organize for Peace, Jewish Voice for Peace Action, and Peace Action PAC confirms he is this community's candidate, while AIPAC's United Democracy Project spent twenty million dollars trying to stop him. His Republican opponent framed the race as a test of Israel loyalty and called refusing to rank Israel a top threat disqualifying, and the Green candidate's anti-war platform, while sharing opposition to U.S. arms flows, lacked the articulated Palestinian self-determination framework El-Sayed laid out.

Ty Pinkins has not called the war in Gaza a genocide and has not demanded an end to U.S. military aid to Israel, and for a federal seat that silence keeps the status quo of arms transfers intact. He is nonetheless the only candidate in this Mississippi United States Senate race who has pushed back. In February 2025 he labeled Trump's Gaza plan reckless and criticized Cindy Hyde-Smith for supporting it; in October 2026 he called the American relationship with Israel's government unhealthy and refused AIPAC money over its influence. Hyde-Smith has spent years defending Israel: she received $257,495 from pro-Israel PACs including AIPAC and United Democracy Project, cosponsored the Antisemitism Awareness Act in 2025, posted in May 2024 that seventy percent of Gazans saw Hamas's October 7 attack as correct, and joined an effort to block Gazan refugees. Pinkins stops at broad policy objection rather than naming a genocide or cutting weapons funding, and that gap is real. Against a senator whose record is a steady, well-funded defense of Israel's military, Pinkins at least opens the question of what this relationship costs.

Alani Bankhead has not called the war in Gaza a genocide and has not backed ending all U.S. military and economic aid to Israel. For a candidate seeking a seat in the United States Senate, that silence effectively upholds the status quo. What she has done is narrower: in October 2026 she supported enforcing the Leahy Law as a full arms embargo on Israel during the assault on Gaza, a conditional step that stops short of cutting off aid entirely. In July 2026, on her Humble Warrior podcast, she told listeners she loves the IDF and Mossad to pieces, a statement that undercuts the October position and signals her primary alignment remains with Israel's military. Her October embargo position is the least-bad lever available to a voter in this race, even though it falls well short of the two tests every voter should be applying: opposing the killing of Palestinians in Gaza and ending the flow of American weapons and dollars to Israel.

For the Nebraska U.S. Senate seat, Dan Osborn has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers to Israel, and his platform opposes reckless foreign wars and Iran spending without specific Palestine or Israel-aid language. For a federal office-seeker, that silence on those questions effectively endorses the status quo of continued U.S. military and economic support for Israel. What separates Osborn from Pete Ricketts is that Ricketts has actively built that status quo: he co-introduced the Stop Support for Hamas Act in October 2023, joined 48 senators affirming Israel's forever survival, proposed defunding the Palestinian Authority, discussed U.S. troop involvement in the Gaza war, and in November 2025 led 25 senators in applauding the exclusion of UNRWA from the peace process. Osborn received and publicly touted an endorsement from a pro-Palestine-aligned group seeking to alter U.S. policy toward Israel by March 2026. Neither has delivered the concrete legislative acts voters need, but one is actively constructing the architecture of the war while the other has broken from that alignment.

Ben Ray Luján is the strongest choice for New Mexico's United States Senate seat because he is the only candidate in this race whose record includes concrete votes against arming Israel. In April 2026 he voted for two Sanders resolutions blocking arms sales to Israel and called the Netanyahu government's war illegal, and in May 2026 he co-signed a Senate letter to CENTCOM questioning whether U.S. forces supported Israel's forced displacement of a million civilians in Lebanon. In January 2024 he voted against tabling a resolution requiring a State Department report on whether Israel was using U.S. weapons to commit human rights violations in Gaza. He has not used the word genocide and does not frame the conflict in those terms; his ceasefire language centers hostage releases. He takes no AIPAC or United Democracy Project money but does accept contributions from J Street, JACPAC, and DMFI. For a voter whose litmus tests are opposing the war in Gaza and ending U.S. military aid to Israel, Luján's April 2026 votes to block arms sales and his willingness to question U.S. military involvement in Lebanon put him ahead of every other name on this ballot.

For the U.S. Senate in North Carolina, Michael Dublin is the only candidate whose positions challenge the machinery of U.S. support for Israel rather than manage it. In March 2024 he called for AIPAC to be registered as a foreign agent and criticized a fellow candidate for opposing a Palestine ceasefire, and his platform extends that with calls for drastic military cuts, NATO abolition, and opposition to imperialism. He has not called the war in Gaza a genocide or backed a named bill blocking weapons transfers. Even so, the alternatives are stark: Roy Cooper rejected a legislative effort to block U.S. military aid to Israel in August 2025, signed the SHALOM Act, and drew nearly ten thousand dollars from pro-Israel PACs including DMFI PAC for this race, while Michael Whatley told the Republican Jewish Coalition he stands by Israel and has taken over three hundred thousand dollars from pro-Israel groups. Dublin is the only one of the three who has named AIPAC's domestic influence as a problem and built a platform around pulling U.S. military power out of the region rather than repositioning it.

For the U.S. Senate seat in Ohio, Greg Levy is the strongest choice. To be clear: Levy has not yet cosponsored a bill to block weapons transfers or voted against an aid package; what he has done is publicly set out positions on Palestine and AIPAC, confirmed by his August 2026 posts, and Vote for Peace rates him an Ally in the general. That distinction matters because the other two candidates have taken the opposite side. Sherrod Brown voted for the April 2024 supplemental military aid to Israel and against all three November 2024 resolutions that would have blocked arms transfers, and his spokesperson affirmed his commitment to funding Israel's war. Jon Husted blocked S.J. Res. 32 and 138 on the floor, keeping D9 bulldozers and 1,000-pound bomb bodies en route to Israel, and took nearly $646,000 from AIPAC and United Democracy Project. Levy is the only candidate in this race who has not voted to arm Israel and who has articulated positions on the conflict. For a federal office where no recorded stance defaults to the status quo, that is the strongest option available.

N'Kiyla Jasmine Thomas is the strongest candidate in Oklahoma's U.S. Senate race. On August 23 she called for an immediate ceasefire in Gaza and pledged to restore USAID funding. Three days later she discarded a bin labeled AIPAC Funds on camera, declaring herself a sole grassroots candidate. Vote for Peace rated her an Ally in the general-election phase. She has not called the war a genocide or backed blocking weapons transfers, and for a federal office-seeker that gap effectively supports the status quo on arms sales. She is still the best choice listed. Kevin Hern has twice called Israel's war righteous and took over $95,000 from AIPAC and allied PACs in this race. Curtis Stinnett named genocide but made continued funding contingent on Netanyahu's removal, leaving resumed aid open. Ron Meinhardt opposes a U.S. war in Iran on Israel's behalf but stops short of a broader aid cutoff. Thomas's ceasefire pledge, her public rejection of AIPAC money, and her pro-Palestine-aligned backing give voters a candidate who will press for a ceasefire rather than defend the bombing.

In the race for Oregon's Senate seat, Jeff Merkley is the stronger choice for voters who want opposition to the killing in Gaza and the weapons flowing to Israel. On November 20, 2024, he spoke on the Senate floor in support of three Joint Resolutions of Disapproval to block offensive weapons sales to the Netanyahu government, and in July 2025 he diverged from Wyden on a vote to block arms sales, taking a more supportive position. In September 2025, he co-authored a twenty-one-page report with Van Hollen calling Israel's actions in Gaza ethnic cleansing and naming the United States complicit. He has not used the word genocide, and his July 2025 floor remarks centered on humanitarian aid. Even so, Merkley is the only candidate here with documented legislative action to block weapons transfers. Gary Dye's single August 2026 post opposing Zionist influence and US support for Israeli wars rests on a Libertarian liberty argument and names no bills or votes. A senator who has spoken on the floor to block arms sales and co-authored a report naming the United States complicit offers a path to accountability a challenger with no legislative record cannot match.

In the 2026 race for United States Senator in Tennessee, Tharon Chandler (I) is the strongest option on the questions that matter most. In a May 2025 Substack post, Chandler explicitly called the Israeli war in Gaza a genocide and framed it as a Zionist plan to obliterate Gaza. Neither opponent has matched that direct condemnation: Bill Hagerty voted against three resolutions that would have blocked weapons sales to Israel during the conflict, co-introduced the UNRWA Reform Act, and had his 2026 re-election backed by an Israel-aligned PAC; Marquita Bradshaw advocated a two-state solution in March 2024 without naming the humanitarian harm, condemning military operations, or calling for an end to U.S. aid. Chandler has not stated a position on blocking U.S. weapons transfers or ending military and economic aid to Israel, and for a federal office-seeker, silence on those questions effectively endorses their continuation. Even so, of the three candidates shown, only Chandler has used the word genocide to describe what is happening in Gaza, and that distinction puts him ahead of opponents who have actively defended Israel's war or spoken only in diplomatic terms.

Brian Bengs is the strongest candidate for South Dakota's U.S. Senate seat because he is the only one on this ballot who has put concrete legal analysis to work on the Gaza question. In September 2025 he published a legal examination titled Is There Genocide In Gaza, and in June 2025 he named the United States as Israel's primary weapons supplier, calling the country partially responsible and stating that Israel lacked legal grounds for its strikes on Iran. He has not called for an end to American military assistance to Israel, and his analysis stops short of declaring genocide proven. But on a ballot where the alternative is a senator who voted against blocking roughly four-fifty million dollars in weapons transfers to Israel in April 2026, who drew one-hundred-seventy thousand dollars from AIPAC-aligned PACs, and who reaffirmed America's commitment to stand with Israel on the October 7 anniversary, Bengs's willingness to question the legal basis of U.S. arms flows and to frame American complicity as a fact rather than an abstraction makes him the clear choice for a voter who wants the Senate to finally interrogate what it is funding.

For the U.S. Senate, James Talarico is the strongest option for voters who want a senator to confront the humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza. He has condemned Netanyahu's use of forced famine and collective punishment and stated Israel has no right to wage war against civilians or restrict aid, calling the suffering there something that makes him sick to his stomach. He has not called the war a genocide or backed ending U.S. military aid, and his position is to condition rather than cut that aid. Even so, he remains the clearest contrast to his opponents. Ken Paxton, as Texas AG, opened a state investigation into pro-Palestinian student walkouts near Dallas and called for firing educators, using state authority to suppress campus solidarity. Paxton vowed to never stop standing with Israel and the Jewish people and took $6,000 from pro-Israel PACs, while Talarico pledged not to accept AIPAC money and drew only $450 from pro-Israel groups. A senator who names collective punishment and conditions aid is a materially different check on the status quo than one who deploys the AG's office against students for supporting Palestinians.

Rachel Fetty Anderson is the strongest choice for the West Virginia Senate seat. She has not called Gaza a genocide or singled out Israel in a specific arms-transfer vote, but she has committed to a two-state solution and stated she would not vote to send or sell weapons to any country except for purely self-defense purposes. In a federal office where no stated position amounts to endorsing the status quo, that principle directly constrains the votes that fund and authorize arms transfers. Neither alternative offers any comparable constraint. Shelley Moore Capito cosponsored the 2025 Antisemitism Awareness Act, which directs the Department of Education to apply the IHRA definition in campus antisemitism investigations — the definitional tool associated with equating criticism of Israel with antisemitism. S. Marshall Wilson frames Israel as the Middle East nation whose worldview best matches the American Founding and offers no engagement with Palestinian justice or the war in Gaza. Anderson is the only candidate here whose stated principle would withhold a weapons vote, and she pairs that with a two-state commitment the others never mention.

For the U.S. House of Representatives CD-1 race, Monica Alponte is the strongest choice. Her platform explicitly opposes U.S. military and financial aid to Israel and rejects AIPAC and all foreign lobbying money, and she pledges never to fund military action without a formal Declaration of War. On September 30, 2026, she publicly defended Palestinian children's pro-Palestine drawings when an Israeli delegation at the UN demanded their removal. She has not yet called the war in Gaza a genocide by name, but her opposition to U.S. military and economic aid and her defense of Palestinian children's expression put her squarely on the right side of the two questions voters must weigh. By contrast, Amish Shah backed Israel's war to destroy Hamas and supported U.S. Iron Dome funding, and his campaign was endorsed by Hindu American PAC, a Hindu-nationalist-aligned group. Jay Feely pledged to stand unapologetically with Israel, called it America's greatest Middle East ally, and declared Hamas must accept Trump's peace deal or face annihilation. Alponte is the only candidate in this race whose documented record opposes the weapons pipeline and defends Palestinian children rather than Israeli military objectives.

For the 2026 United States House of Representatives race in CD-2, Shomari Figures (D) has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers, and has not voted against arms-funding or aid bills, and in a federal seat, taking no recorded position on those questions effectively supports the status quo. Vote for Peace, a human rights and war-lobby funding guide, nonetheless rates Figures as an Ally in this contest, and his campaign platform centers on concrete domestic commitments—Medicaid expansion, SNAP and Social Security protection, rural infrastructure, student-loan relief, and preservation of African American civil rights landmarks such as the Freedom Rides Museum and Tuskegee Airmen monument. His opponent, Rhett Marques (R), pledges to strongly support Israel as a Christian and American, frames that backing as a religious and patriotic duty, and commits to the administration's push for sustainable peace in the Middle East while offering no reference to Palestinian rights. Between a candidate whose silence on the war at least does not carry an explicit pro-Israel pledge and one who makes that pledge a headline of his platform, Figures is the stronger choice on the record shown.

In the November 2026 race for a U.S. House seat in California's Sixth District, Richard Pan has not called the war in Gaza a genocide and has not backed blocking weapons transfers to Israel; his platform calls generically for ending wars without naming Israel, and at the August 2026 Sacramento Bee debate he declined a yes-or-no answer on whether Israel committed genocide while affirming Israel's right to exist and defend itself. For a federal office, that silence effectively means supporting continued U.S. military and economic aid to Israel. Yet Pan is the stronger option listed here. Kevin Kiley traveled to Israel in April 2024 on an AIPAC-organized delegation, praised Yale's overnight crackdown on pro-Palestine encampments in April 2025, voted Yea on bills incorporating the IHRA definition into federal education law, and drew over $74,000 from pro-Israel PACs in the 2026 cycle. CAIR Action lists Pan as preferred, a tier below full endorsement, and Pan at least framed the conflict around a humanitarian crisis, a lens entirely absent from Kiley's record.

Randy Villegas is the stronger choice for U.S. Representative in California's 22nd district. He has recognized the genocide in Gaza and pledged to oppose military aid to Israel, as confirmed by Track AIPAC in September 2026, and earlier signed a public ceasefire letter to the White House in January 2024. CAIR Action endorsed him for this race. David Valadao, by contrast, co-introduced a House resolution supporting Israel's right to defend itself in October 2023, voted for emergency military funding to Israel in November 2023, and earned a direct AIPAC PAC endorsement for this 2026 contest. Pro-Israel spenders DMFI PAC and the UDP-funded 314 Action Fund ran ads against Villegas, underscoring how firmly he opposes the aid pipeline. On both litmus tests—naming what is happening in Gaza a genocide and pledging to end U.S. military aid—Villegas has taken concrete action, while Valadao voted to fund it.

For Colorado's third congressional district in November 2026, Clifton Brown is the only candidate on this ballot who calls the US-backed attack on Gaza a genocide and pledges to stop funding Israel and end US arms sales worldwide. Those are campaign platform commitments rather than legislative votes, and he has not yet cosponsored a blocking bill or voted against an appropriations measure, but they put him squarely on both sides of the question voters care about most. Dwayne Romero, the Democrat, said in June 2026 that he supports US military funding for Israel from a defensive perspective, keeping the aid relationship intact and stopping short of a ceasefire demand. Jeff Hurd, the Republican, called the Israel-Hamas ceasefire a turning point for hostage return in October 2025, took an AIPAC-organized trip to Tel Aviv in August 2025 to meet Prime Minister Netanyahu, and in 2026 accepted over $104,000 from AIPAC's PAC and the United Democracy Project. Vote for Peace, a pro-Palestine-aligned group, rated Hurd opposed. Brown is the strongest option listed because he alone names the violence for what it is and commits in writing to ending the financial and military support that fuels it.

Barnett is the Muslim community's candidate for the U.S. House seat in Michigan's 4th district, and her confirmed alignment with Palestinian justice makes her the only candidate in this race whose community commitment points toward the people of Gaza. She has not yet cast a recorded vote on blocking weapons transfers or called the war a genocide, and for a federal office-seeker, the absence of such a position leaves the current flow of U.S. military and economic aid to Israel intact. Even so, she is the strongest option available. McCann said he would take a look at continuing U.S. military aid without committing to end it, and his campaign carries Israel-aligned endorsements from major labor and professional organizations. Huizenga voted to shield Israel from congressional scrutiny on Gaza and to embed the IHRA framework in federal education enforcement. Barnett, grounded in the pro-Palestine Muslim community, is the candidate most positioned to break that pattern once seated.

Vote for Manny Rutinel for Colorado's 8th District congressional seat. In 2022 Rutinel called Israel's actions in Gaza a genocide and advocated for a ceasefire, citing his Palestinian heritage. He has not, however, backed blocking weapons transfers to Israel or ended U.S. military and economic aid, and for a federal candidate that silence effectively endorses the status quo on arms funding. A UDP-linked spending group, 314 Action Fund, poured nearly two hundred thousand dollars into independent ads supporting Rutinel, a funding pattern that signals alignment with Israel-lobby interests, and he accepted eighteen thousand dollars from pro-Israel PACs in the 2026 cycle. The alternative, Gabe Evans, introduced a resolution in June 2025 branding Free Palestine an antisemitic slogan, posted on the October 7 anniversary in 2026 that he stands with Israel and Colorado's Jewish community, and collected roughly eighty-five thousand dollars from pro-Israel PACs including AIPAC. Vote for Peace, a Muslim-community-aligned group, opposed Evans in the general. Rutinel is the stronger choice: he named the violence for what it is, while Evans legislated to suppress the words used to name it.

In the November 2026 race for U.S. House of Representatives in Michigan's 7th District, William Lawrence (D) has made opposing the genocide in Gaza and stopping U.S. arms sales to Israel the core of his campaign. At a June 2026 Latino community forum, Lawrence explicitly called Israel's attacks on Gaza genocide, and by July he had built his entire run around that opposition. He publicly challenged opponents who refused to answer whether Israel committed genocide, describing them as in the pocket of the pro-war lobby. Vote for Peace rated Lawrence an Ally, and his stance drew roughly $1 million in opposition spending from DMFI through Rolling Sea PAC. His main opponent, Tom Barrett (R), has declared he will always stand with Israel as the nation's strongest ally, urged Michigan State University to adopt the IHRA working definition of antisemitism, and has drawn nearly $60,000 in 2026 from pro-Israel PACs including AIPAC and the Republican Jewish Coalition, while Vote for Peace rated him Opposed. For voters measuring candidates on opposing Gaza's genocide and cutting off weapons to Israel, Lawrence is the clear choice.

Sam Forstag is the candidate in this race for United States Representative who has taken a concrete, dated stand on the two questions that matter most to voters. On May 24, 2026, he publicly stated that he would not vote for an appropriations package sending weapons to Israel and called the situation in Gaza a genocide. That is not a vague pledge or a conditional position; it is a specific refusal to fund arms transfers paired with a direct moral judgment on the ongoing killing. If you want a member of Congress who will vote against the weapons pipeline and name what is happening for what it is, he is the candidate who has already put that on the record.

Jamie Ager is the strongest option on the ballot for the United States House of Representatives seat in the eleventh district. Vote for Peace, which evaluates candidates on human rights and war-lobby funding, rates her as an Ally, a tier reflecting concrete, documented stances in support of Palestinian justice. That is a meaningful distinction in this race. But a voter is owed transparency: Jamie Ager has not called the killing of Palestinians in Gaza a genocide, has not cosponsored legislation to block weapons transfers to Israel, and has not voted against U.S. military or economic aid to Israel. For a member of Congress, having no recorded position on whether a population is being destroyed and whether American tax dollars are funding that destruction is not neutrality; it is support for the status quo. Even so, her documented Ally-tier alignment on Palestinian justice is the clearest pro-Palestinian signal a voter will find in this race, and that makes her the strongest choice available.

For the United States House of Representatives race in Nebraska's second district, Denise Powell is the strongest available choice. In April 2026 she rejected an ad purchase from Democratic Majority for Israel, and in May she disavowed all Israel-focused outside groups, after which DMFI canceled its spending in the race. Jewish Insider identified Powell as the Israel critic in her Democratic primary. Yet her foreign-policy platform addresses China and Russia without naming Israel or Palestine, and she has not called the killing in Gaza a genocide, blocked weapons transfers, or backed divestment from Israeli companies. In a federal seat, no recorded position on aid and arms effectively endorses the status quo. What sets Powell apart is that she is the only candidate here with a researched record, and she took a concrete public stand against Israel-aligned spending in her own race. Meanwhile, AIPAC-backed super PACs BOLD America and EDW Action Fund spent over $600,000 supporting her in October despite her disavowal, underscoring the financial pressure these groups exert on this seat.

Stefany Shaheen is the strongest choice for New Hampshire's first congressional district because she took concrete action to end U.S. military aid to Israel, backing the Massie Amendment in August 2026 to block that funding after initially declining to state her position, and she built her September primary victory on opposition to Israeli military aid and an anti-AIPAC campaign. She has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, a shortfall that sits in tension with her legislative action. Still, she donated $29,650 from AIPAC-adjacent donors to three New Hampshire community health centers rather than retaining that money for her campaign, and she publicly attacked her opponent over donations from 150 AIPAC supporters. Anthony DiLorenzo, by contrast, told a GOP primary audience in August 2026 that he supports Israel, attaching only a vague humanitarian-condition qualifier to his backing, and his campaign carries an AIPAC-linked donation on file. Shaheen is the only candidate in this race who moved to cut off military funding to Israel and made that position the center of her candidacy.

For the U.S. House seat in CD-2, Teresa Benitez-Thompson has not called the killing in Gaza a genocide or voted to block weapons transfers to Israel, and for a federal candidate that silence effectively preserves the current arms pipeline. What she has committed to is more than any other candidate here has offered: conditioning military aid on compliance with international humanitarian law, phasing out offensive arms sales, funding UNRWA aid, ending settlement expansion, and pursuing a two-state framework. She keeps Iron Dome funding, a real limit, but her direction is toward accountability rather than unconditional defense of an ally. David Flippo, carrying an AIPAC endorsement, blamed Hamas for the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, told a Real America's Voice audience that Hamas does not want to be part of society, and claimed credit for food deliveries that records attribute to the Order of St. John. Between a candidate who has not yet acted and one who misattributes humanitarian work while defending the status quo, Benitez-Thompson is the stronger choice.

Seamus O'Toole runs for the U.S. House of Representatives in New Jersey's seventh district under the Stop Israel's Genocide party banner, explicitly naming the war in Gaza a genocide and opposing Israel's conduct. He has not yet voted on arms funding or backed blocking weapons transfers, as a new candidate without a legislative record. But no other candidate in this race calls the war what it is. Thomas Kean Jr. holds an AIPAC endorsement, voted yes on the $14.3 billion Israel Security Supplemental Appropriations Act containing no Palestinian humanitarian aid, and voted yes on H.R. 6090 directing the IHRA definition into education enforcement. Rebecca Bennett welcomed the return of hostages and called for humanitarian aid in Gaza but never named Israeli military action or a ceasefire, while drawing JStreet PAC support and over $85,000 from pro-Israel PACs. O'Toole is the only candidate in this race whose entire platform is built on naming the genocide and opposing Israel's conduct, making him the clear choice for voters who will not accept vague calls for peace while U.S. weapons keep falling.

In the race for U.S. House Representative CD-7, Brian Poindexter's platform identifies ending the war in Iran as a step toward lower energy prices, reflecting a broader anti-war stance in the Middle East, and he carries the endorsement of Congressman Ro Khanna from the Muslim-community and pro-Palestine-aligned side. He has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers, and has not voted against U.S. military or economic aid to Israel; for a federal office-seeker, that absence of action effectively supports the status quo. His only documented Gaza statement, from August 2026, framed the conflict through a military-benefits lens. Against Max Miller, who in June 2025 called himself a proud Jewish American and staunch defender of Israel, co-led reintroduction of the Antisemitism Awareness Act, and drew $473,207 from pro-Israel PACs including AIPAC PAC and United Democracy Project, Poindexter's anti-war positioning and funding chiefly from J Street PAC rather than AIPAC make him the clearer choice for voters who want the broader Middle East war to end.

For the U.S. House seat in Ohio's 15th district, voters should support Don Leonard. In an April 2026 interview with D.J. Byrnes, Leonard weighed the terms act of war, crimes against humanity, and genocide to characterize Israel's conduct in Gaza, and by October 2026 he calls the slaughter in Gaza a genocide and supports a full arms embargo. Vote for Peace backs him in the general election. His Republican opponent, Mike Carey, voted yes on the Antisemitism Awareness Act in May 2024, embedding the IHRA definition in federal education-discrimination law, cosponsored a resolution honoring two Israeli embassy employees killed in Washington, and in October 2025 framed ending the war as a response to the October 7 Hamas attack while praising the President's ceasefire leadership. Carey took over ninety-two thousand dollars from AIPAC PAC and its super PAC United Democracy Project, plus another thirty-four thousand from AIPAC directly, per FEC filings. Leonard has not cosponsored a blocking-bombs bill or voted against a named arms-funding appropriation, but he has named the act genocide and backed a full embargo. Carey built his campaign on AIPAC money while praising the President's handling of the war rather than demanding an end to U.S. weapons transfers.

For the U.S. House race in Texas's 28th District, Marlon Duran is the strongest option because his platform grounds Palestinian justice in the same anti-oppression framework as South Africa's anti-apartheid struggle and the indigenous-rights fight in South Texas, calling for international law and human dignity to govern American policy. On March 14, 2026, he pledged he will never accept money from AIPAC or any PAC. To be clear, Duran has not yet voted against arms transfers, cosponsored a block-the-bombs measure, or called the situation a genocide, and in a federal seat the absence of those concrete acts effectively leaves the current aid relationship in place.
